title: Service health quickstart playbook for feature teams
summary: A lightweight, pragmatic playbook to help product/feature teams adopt SLOs and basic reliability practices in a single 1-week sprint. Focus: measurable guardrails, minimal alerts, and clear handoffs to SRE for escalation.
content:
Purpose:
This is a working quickstart for feature teams who need to ship a new feature or service while meeting basic reliability guarantees. The goal is not to produce perfect SLOs, but to create pragmatic, measurable guardrails that protect user experience and enable predictable incident response.

Who this is for:
- Feature/product teams (frontend, backend, infra-dependent) launching within the next 4–8 weeks.
- Partnering SREs and on-call owners who will advise and accept escalations.

Outcome in 1 week (accelerator sprint):
- One service-level objective (SLO) defined and applied to a measurable signal (latency or error-rate).
- Error budget policy and simple alert thresholds submitted as a PR.
- Basic runbook stub + escalation points created in team repo.
- Ops handoff meeting with SRE and follow-up tickets created.

3-step approach (micro-SLO):
1) Pick the user-facing contract: what matters? (e.g., API success rate, 95th percentile latency for interactive endpoints, embedding generation throughput).
2) Instrument and baseline: add counters, timers (Prometheus histogram & example labels). Run a 48h baseline to measure p50/p95 and error rates.
3) Set guardrail SLO: pick an SLO and error budget policy that the team can reasonably achieve after 1 sprint (example: 99.5% success rate over 7d for non-critical batch; 99.9% for interactive read).

One-week sprint template (day-by-day):
- Day 0 (prep): create a tracking ticket (use JIRA-REL-312 template), identify SRE buddy, add monitoring stub in codebase.
- Day 1: instrument critical paths (metrics + distributed trace context). Start 48h baseline collection.
- Day 2: draft SLO statement + rationale in repo: "SLO: 99.5% success over 7d for /v1/generate". Add sample alert thresholds.
- Day 3: PR monitoring config + runbook stub. Request SRE review.
- Day 4: tabletop: run a 30m incident playthrough with SRE. Iterate runbook.
- Day 5: ops handoff meeting, finalize follow-ups, merge monitoring PR.

Minimal SLO template (single sentence):
- "Objective: 99.5% successful responses for endpoint X measured over 7 days (success = HTTP 2xx and no downstream timeout)."
- "Indicator: count(success) / count(total) per service instance, tag by region and deployment."

Alerting & error budget policy (example):
- Page at p95 latency > 1.5s sustained for 10m OR 5xx rate > 1% for 5m.
- Page SRE if error budget burn rate > 3x for a rolling 1h window.
- Create Jira ticket if weekly availability droops below SLO for 2 consecutive weeks.

Runbook stub checklist (to include in PR):
- Symptoms (what users see).
- Quick triage steps (service health dashboard, common logs, recent deploys).
- Known mitigations (toggle feature flags, scale pools, fallback model).
- Escalation contacts (primary oncall, SRE buddy, product owner).
- Post-incident action owner (who will file RCA).

Operational notes and tips:
- Start with a single signal (latency or success). Too many SLOs = paralysis.
- Use 7–14 day windows during early adoption; move to 28d after stable baselines.
- Prefer broader SLOs (service-level) over endpoint-level for v0; refine later.
- Cache and batching changes can drastically alter token-level costs — note expected cost delta when changing request patterns.

Cross-functional coordination (roles & handshake):
- Product/Feature: defines user impact and accepts tradeoffs.
- Engineering owner: instruments metrics and creates PR.
- SRE: advises on thresholds, reviews monitoring PR, and owns escalation policy.
- QA: provides load test scenarios for the 48h baseline.
- Data/Observability: ensures dashboards and traces show meaningful slowness/error dimensions.

Communication plan:
- Kickoff: 30m with SRE within 24h of sprint start.
- Daily stand: 10m quick sync for 5 days.
- Tabletop: 30m mid-sprint.
- Handoff: 45m final review + acceptance criteria sign-off.

Decision log (what to capture in PR description):
- Chosen SLO and why (user story).
- Baseline numbers and sample queries used.
- Tradeoffs considered (e.g., lenient SLO to avoid throttling vs stricter SLO to protect UX).
- Follow-up work and owners.

Unresolved questions / TODOs:
- Should we standardize a template for "success" across client types? (Maya to propose by 2026-06-05).
- Which teams want automated weekly SLO reports? (Tally in spreadsheet linked in CON-1428).

Quick links and templates:
- Monitoring config PR example: https://github.com/redwood-inference/monitoring-configs/pull/87
- JIRA template: JIRA-REL-312
- Confluence binder with longer SLO guidance: CON-1428-service-health-templates

Notes to self (informal):
- Keep this as a "one-feature" onboarding: success = teams ship with a minimal SLO AND a working runbook.
- Expect to refine thresholds after first 2 weeks of production traffic.
- Avoid building long dashboards up-front — start with a single panel that answers "is the feature healthy?"

Next steps / owners:
- Avery: publish this playbook to CON-1428 and link PR template (due 2026-06-07).
- Maya: propose concrete "success" definition for SDK vs API by 2026-06-05.
- Liam: add example Prometheus queries and dashboard JSON to monitoring-configs repo (PR by 2026-06-10).

Appendix: sample PromQL (starter):
- request_success_rate = sum(rate(http_requests_total{endpoint="/v1/generate",code=~"2.."}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{endpoint="/v1/generate"}[5m]))
- p95_latency = histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(http_request_latency_bucket{endpoint="/v1/generate"}[5m])) by (le))

End of doc.

(Working draft — feedback welcome; this is intentionally lightweight and actionable.)
